paper_sections.title: Neural Correlates of Suppressing Distractor Interference at Low Perceptual Load
Neural Correlates of Suppressing Distractor Interference at High Perceptual Load

description.value: A functional MRI study of distractor interference during visual target identification under low and high perceptual load, examining load-dependent changes in whole-brain BOLD activity in 24 healthy adults.

spans.text: We studied 24 healthy participants using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) during a visual target identification task with two perceptual loads (low vs. high).

description.value: Non-interventional, repeated-measures 2×2 factorial study with low versus high perceptual load and distractor versus no-distractor conditions. Participants performed three functional runs; block order was randomized within runs and run order was counterbalanced across participants.

spans.text: The task used a 2×2 factorial design with two perceptual loads (low, high) and two distractor conditions (with, without).
Within each run, each blocked condition was repeated four times, and the whole run lasted 387.2s.
During scanning, each subject performed three functional runs using three different task scripts.

spans.text: Stimuli for each condition were grouped into blocks with the same 16 faces used in every trial block.
Stimulus presentation was implemented with Psychtoolbox (  http://psychtoolbox.org/PTB-2/osx.html  ) and displayed on the screen of a Macintosh laptop.

instructions.value: Please identify, followed by an instruction image specifying the facial features defining targets in the upcoming block.

spans.text: The instruction, “Please identify,” was presented for 5 s before each trial block above an instruction image specifying the facial features for the targets in the following task block ( Fig. 1 ).

stimuli.value: Sixteen schematic faces as targets and 64 scene pictures as background distractors.

spans.text: The task used 16 schematic faces as targets and 64 scene pictures as background distractors ( Fig. 1 ).
Participants were required to identify targets specified for each block and to respond by pressing a button as soon as possible after detecting a target.
Task performance was assessed using reaction time (RT), rate of omission error, and rate of commission error.
